title: In the Beginning
subtitle: Genesis 1 to 3, Berean Standard Bible
description: The creation of the world, Eden, and the first human choices.
paragraphs: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth."
The earth was formless and void. Darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.
God spoke, and there was light. He separated the light from the darkness and called the light day and the darkness night. Evening came, then morning. The first day was done.
He made the sky and separated the waters above it from the waters below it. The second day was done.

He gathered the waters under the sky into one place, and dry land appeared. He called the dry land earth and the gathered waters seas. The earth brought forth seed-bearing plants and fruit trees, each after its kind. The third day was done.

He set lights in the sky to separate day from night and to mark seasons, days, and years. The greater light ruled the day. The lesser light ruled the night. He made the stars as well. The fourth day was done.
The waters filled with living creatures, and birds flew above the earth. God blessed them and told them to be fruitful and multiply. The fifth day was done.

The earth brought forth livestock, beasts, and every creature that crawls on the ground, each after its kind. Then God made man in His own image, male and female, blessed them, and gave them the earth to fill and rule. He saw all that He had made, and it was very good. The sixth day was done.
On the seventh day God rested from all His work. He blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.
Now the story comes down to the man himself.
The LORD God formed him from the dust of the ground. God breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being.

The man was placed in a garden God had planted in Eden, in the east. No rain had fallen on the earth yet. Springs welled up from the ground and watered it. In the garden, trees grew that were pleasing to the eye and good for food. In the middle of the garden stood the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divided into four rivers, the Pishon, the Gihon, the Tigris, and the Euphrates.
The man had work there. He was put in the garden to cultivate it and keep it.

He also had a command to learn. God told him he could eat freely from every tree in the garden. From one tree he could not eat. It was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. In the day he ate from it, he would surely die.
God said, "It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper."
Then the animals came to the man.

God had formed every beast of the field and every bird of the air out of the ground, and He brought them to the man to see what he would call each one. The man gave names to all the livestock. He gave names to the birds of the air. He gave names to every beast of the field. Whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name.

Name after name was spoken in that garden. Creature after creature passed in front of him. When the naming was done, the result stood plain in front of him. For Adam no suitable helper had been found.
God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep.
While he slept, God took one of the man's ribs and closed up the place with flesh. From the rib He made a woman. Then God brought her to the man.
The man woke to someone who had not been there before he slept. She was made from him, and she was not another animal he had named. He spoke at once.
"This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called 'woman,' for out of man she was taken."
For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh. The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
In the garden with them was the serpent. He was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made.
The serpent spoke to the woman. His first move was a question.
"Did God really say, 'You must not eat from any tree in the garden?'"

The woman answered what she had been told. They could eat the fruit of the trees of the garden. About the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God had said they must not eat it or touch it, or they would die.
The serpent contradicted God to her face. She would not surely die, he told her. God knew that in the day she ate from it, her eyes would be opened and she would be like God, knowing good and evil.
The woman looked at the tree in front of her. She saw that it was good for food. She saw that it was pleasing to the eyes. She saw that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom.
She took its fruit and ate it. She gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate it.
At once their eyes were opened. They knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.
Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day. They hid themselves from His presence among the trees of the garden.
God called to the man. "Where are you?"
The man answered from where he was hiding. He had heard God's voice in the garden. He was afraid because he was naked, so he hid himself.
God asked who had told him he was naked. God asked if he had eaten from the tree He commanded him not to eat from.
The man pointed to the woman. The woman whom God gave him, she gave him fruit from the tree, and he ate it.
God asked the woman what she had done.
She said the serpent deceived her, and she ate.

God dealt with them in order. He spoke to the serpent first. Because he had done this, he was cursed above all livestock and every beast of the field. On his belly he would go, and dust he would eat, all the days of his life. God would put enmity between him and the woman, and between his seed and her seed. He would crush the serpent's head, and the serpent would strike his heel.
To the woman, God said He would sharply increase her pain in childbirth. In pain she would bring forth children. Her desire would be for her husband, and he would rule over her.

To Adam, God said the ground was cursed because of him. He had listened to the voice of his wife and eaten from the tree God commanded him not to eat from. Through toil he would eat of the ground all the days of his life. The ground would yield thorns and thistles for him. By the sweat of his brow he would eat his bread, until he returned to the ground from which he was taken. For dust he was, and to dust he would return.
Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.
God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.

Then Adam learned the last hard fact of that day. God said the man had become like one of Them, knowing good and evil. Now he could not be allowed to reach out his hand, take also from the tree of life, eat, and live forever.

The LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken. He drove the man out. At the east side of the garden He stationed cherubim and a whirling sword of flame, set there to guard the way to the tree of life.

title: Cain and Abel
subtitle: Genesis 4 to 6, Berean Standard Bible
description: Two brothers, the generations beyond Eden, and a world awaiting Noah.
paragraphs: East of Eden, life went on outside the guarded garden.

Adam and Eve had children. Generations would pass, families would spread across the earth, and the ground God had cursed would have to be worked by hand. But the story slows down first for two brothers, because what happened between them showed how fast trouble had moved from a garden to a field.
The older brother was Cain. The younger was Abel.
Adam had relations with his wife Eve, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain. She said, "With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man."
Later she gave birth to Cain's brother Abel.
The brothers grew into different work. Abel kept sheep. Cain tilled the soil.
In the course of time, both brothers brought an offering to the LORD. Cain brought some of the fruit of the soil. Abel brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock.
The LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering. He had no regard for Cain and his offering.
Cain saw the difference. He became very angry, and his countenance fell.
God spoke to him before he did anything else.

"Why are you angry," said the LORD to Cain, "and why has your countenance fallen? If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you refuse to do what is right, sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it."
The warning was in front of Cain, plain and direct. He still called his brother out.
Cain said to his brother Abel, "Let us go out to the field."
While they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.
Abel was dead. Cain stood in a field with no brother beside him, and then God's voice came again.
The LORD said to Cain, "Where is your brother Abel?"
Cain answered, "I do not know! Am I my brother's keeper?"

God knew what the field held. "What have you done?" He said. "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground. Now you are cursed and banished from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. When you till the ground, it will no longer yield its produce to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth."
Cain's own work had turned against him. The soil he tilled would not produce for him, and the earth he lived on would not give him a settled place.

Cain said his punishment was greater than he could bear. God had driven him from the face of the earth. He would be hidden from God's face. He would be a fugitive and a wanderer, and whoever found him would kill him.
The LORD answered, "Not so! If anyone slays Cain, then Cain will be avenged sevenfold."
God placed a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.
Cain went out from the presence of the LORD. He settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.

Life kept building in Cain's line. Cain had a son named Enoch, and Cain built a city and named the city after his son. Generations followed. Irad was born to Enoch. Irad was the father of Mehujael. Mehujael was the father of Methusael. Methusael was the father of Lamech.

Lamech married two women, Adah and Zillah. Adah gave birth to Jabal, the father of those who dwell in tents and raise livestock. Jabal's brother Jubal was the father of all who play the harp and flute. Zillah gave birth to Tubal-cain, a forger of every implement of bronze and iron. His sister was Naamah.

Then Lamech spoke to his wives, and his words were a boast about killing. He had slain a man for wounding him, a young man for striking him. If Cain was avenged sevenfold, Lamech said, then Lamech would be avenged seventy-sevenfold.
Adam and Eve had another son. Eve named him Seth, saying, "God has granted me another seed in place of Abel, since Cain killed him."
Seth had a son and called him Enosh. At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD.

The years ran long in Seth's line. Adam lived 930 years and died. Seth lived 912 years and died. Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, and Jared followed, father to son, and each man lived, had other sons and daughters, and died.

One name breaks the pattern when the reader reaches him. Enoch became the father of Methuselah at 65 years old. After that, Enoch walked with God 300 years. His total years were 365. Then the line changes its rhythm. Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away.

Methuselah lived 969 years, longer than anyone else in the list, and died. His son Lamech had a son at 182 years old and named him Noah, saying, "May this one comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed."
Noah grew. After Noah was 500 years old, he became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

By then men had begun to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born to them. The sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose. The LORD said His Spirit would not contend with man forever, for man is mortal, and his days would be 120 years. The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and afterward as well. Their children became the mighty men of old, men of renown.

Then the reader is shown what God saw. The wickedness of man was great upon the earth. Every inclination of the thoughts of man's heart was altogether evil all the time. The LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart.

God said He would blot out man, whom He had created, from the face of the earth. Man and beast and crawling creature and bird of the air would be blotted out, for God was grieved that He had made them.
The sentence stood over the whole earth. One man stood out inside it.
"Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD."

title: Noah and the Flood
subtitle: Genesis 6 to 9, Berean Standard Bible
description: Noah, the ark, the flood, the dove, and the covenant marked by the rainbow.
paragraphs: Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD. Now the reader learns what set him apart in the world he lived in.
Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God. He had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

The earth around him was corrupt in the sight of God, and it was full of violence. God looked upon the earth and saw that it was corrupt, for all living creatures on the earth had corrupted their ways.
Then God spoke to Noah.
He told Noah the end of all living creatures had come before Him, because through them the earth was full of violence. God would destroy both them and the earth.
Noah's work started with measurements.
God told him, "Make for yourself an ark of gopher wood; make rooms in the ark and coat it with pitch inside and out."

The ark was to be 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. Noah was to make a roof for it, finish its walls a cubit from the top, place a door in its side, and build lower, middle, and upper decks.
God told him why the ark had to hold so much. God would bring floodwaters upon the earth to destroy every creature under the heavens that had the breath of life. Everything on the earth would perish.

Inside that sentence came a promise Noah had not heard before. God would establish His covenant with Noah. Noah would enter the ark with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives. He was to bring two of every living creature into the ark, male and female, to keep them alive with him. Two of every kind of bird, animal, and crawling creature would come to him to be kept alive. He was to take every kind of food that is eaten and gather it for himself and for the animals.
Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him.

Then the LORD spoke again. Noah was to go into the ark, he and all his family, because God had found him righteous in this generation. He was to take seven pairs of every kind of clean animal, a male and its mate, a pair of every kind of unclean animal, and seven pairs of every kind of bird of the air, male and female, to preserve their offspring on the face of all the earth. In seven days God would send rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights, and He would wipe from the face of the earth every living thing He had made.
Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him.

Noah was 600 years old when the floodwaters came upon the earth. He entered the ark with his wife, his sons, and their wives, to escape the waters. The clean and unclean animals, the birds, and everything that crawls along the ground came to Noah and entered the ark two by two, male and female, as God had commanded him. Then the LORD shut him in.

After seven days, the floodwaters came. In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, on the seventeenth day of the second month, all the fountains of the great deep burst forth and the floodgates of the heavens were opened. Rain fell on the earth for forty days and forty nights.

The water did not stop at riverbanks. For forty days the flood kept coming, and the waters rose and lifted the ark high above the earth. The waters surged and rose greatly, and the ark floated on the surface. The waters prevailed until all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered. The waters rose and covered the mountaintops to a depth of fifteen cubits.

Every living thing that moved on the earth perished: birds, livestock, animals, every creature that swarms on the earth, and all mankind. Everything on dry land that had the breath of life in its nostrils died. Every living thing on the face of the earth was blotted out. Only Noah remained, and those with him in the ark.
The waters prevailed on the earth for 150 days.
Noah did not learn the state of the world all at once. He learned it in stages, the way a man sealed inside an ark would have to learn it.

But God remembered Noah, and all the animals and livestock that were with him in the ark. God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside. The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the heavens were closed, and the rain from the sky was restrained. The waters receded steadily from the earth. After 150 days the waters had gone down.

On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. The waters continued to recede until the tenth month. On the first day of the tenth month, the tops of the mountains became visible.

After forty days Noah opened the window he had made in the ark and sent out a raven. The raven kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth. The raven told him nothing clear.

Then Noah sent out a dove to see if the waters had receded from the surface of the ground. The dove found no place to rest her foot. She returned to him in the ark, because the waters were still covering the surface of all the earth. Noah reached out his hand and brought her back inside.
He waited seven more days and sent the dove out again. This time she came back in the evening. In her beak was a freshly plucked olive leaf. Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth.
He waited seven more days and sent the dove out again. This time she did not return to him.

In Noah's six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters had dried up from the earth. Noah removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry. By the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth was fully dry.

Then God told Noah to come out of the ark, with his wife, his sons, and their wives. He was to bring out all the living creatures with him, so they could spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply on it.
Noah came out. His sons, his wife, and his sons' wives came out with him. Every living creature, every creeping thing, and every bird came out of the ark, kind by kind.
Noah built an altar to the LORD. Taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar.

The LORD smelled the pleasing aroma and said in His heart that He would never again curse the ground because of man, even though every inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth. He would never again destroy all living creatures as He had done. As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night would never cease.

God blessed Noah and his sons. He told them to be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. The fear and dread of them would fall on every living creature, and all creatures were delivered into their hand. Everything that lives and moves would be food for them, just as God had given them the green plants. They must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it. God would require an accounting from anyone who took the life of his fellow man, for in the image of God, God had made mankind.

Then Noah heard the word covenant spoken over his whole family, and over every living creature that had come out of the ark with him. God established His covenant with Noah, his descendants after him, and every living creature. "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood; never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth."

God gave a sign for the covenant. "I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth." Whenever clouds formed over the earth and the rainbow appeared in the clouds, God would remember the covenant between Him and every living creature. The waters would never again become a flood to destroy all life.
Noah's three sons were the men from whom the whole earth was populated. Shem, Ham, and Japheth came out of the ark, and Ham was the father of Canaan.

After the flood, Noah, a man of the soil, planted a vineyard. When he drank some of its wine, he became drunk and uncovered himself inside his tent. Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside.

Shem and Japheth took a garment and placed it across their shoulders. Walking backward, they covered their father's nakedness. Their faces were turned away, so they did not see their father's nakedness.

When Noah awoke from his drunkenness, he learned what his youngest son had done to him. He cursed Canaan, saying Canaan would be a servant of servants to his brothers. He blessed the LORD, the God of Shem, and said Canaan would be the servant of Shem. He asked God to expand the territory of Japheth, that Japheth would dwell in the tents of Shem, and that Canaan would be his servant.
After the flood Noah lived 350 years. He lived a total of 950 years, and then he died.
The earth had a population again, and it all traced back to three brothers who had walked out of the ark.

title: Nations and Babel
subtitle: Genesis 10 to 11, Berean Standard Bible
description: The nations after the flood, the tower at Babel, and the family line that leads to Abram.
paragraphs: The ark had emptied into a world that needed people again.

Genesis does not rush past that filling. It names the sons of Noah and follows their families outward: Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and then sons, grandsons, towns, coastlands, and nations. The reader meets the world the way Noah's descendants would have met it, one family at a time, with new names spreading farther from the ark than anyone in Noah's house had ever lived.

Japheth's line moved toward the coastlands. From his sons came peoples divided by land and language, maritime peoples who spread into their territories. Ham's line ran through Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan. In that line Genesis pauses on Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD and the first on earth to be a mighty man. His kingdom began with Babel in the land of Shinar, and from that land he went to Assyria and built Nineveh and other great cities. Egypt's line produced peoples whose names later fill Israel's story. Canaan's line reached from Sidon toward Gerar and Gaza, and toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim. The map is already carrying trouble in some of its names.

Shem's line carried the family line forward. Shem was the father of Eber, and through Eber the line moved toward Peleg. In Peleg's days the earth was divided. Genesis gives the sentence without stopping to explain it, then keeps walking the line down toward Terah. By the end of the list, the whole earth has been populated from Noah's sons, clan by clan, language by language, land by land.
Then the story pulls back to a plain in Shinar.

At that time the whole earth had one language and the same words. As people migrated from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. They made bricks to use for stone and used tar for mortar. The work gave them an idea larger than shelter.

They said they would build a city for themselves, and a tower with its top in the heavens. They wanted to make a name for themselves. They did not want to be scattered over the face of the whole earth.
The building rose from a settled people who had one speech and one plan. Then the LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of men were building.

The LORD said, "If they have begun to do this as one people speaking the same language, then nothing they devise will be beyond them. Come, let Us go down and confuse their language, so that they will not understand one another's speech."

The work stopped in the middle of human speech. A worker could call for brick, mortar, help, or time to rest, and the man beside him could not understand the words. The LORD scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they stopped building the city.
Its name became Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of the whole earth. The scattering the builders feared came from the place where they tried to prevent it.
Genesis has just filled the earth with nations. Now it narrows again.

The line of Shem continues in names and ages. Arphaxad. Shelah. Eber. Peleg. Reu. Serug. Nahor. Terah. Fathers live, sons are born, years stack up, and the wide map begins to tighten around one household. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran became the father of Lot, then Haran died in Ur of the Chaldeans, in the land of his birth, while his father Terah was still living.
Abram married Sarai. Nahor married Milcah, the daughter of Haran. Sarai was barren. She had no child.

Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, and they set out from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. They did not reach Canaan. They came to Haran and settled there.
Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran.

So the nations covered the earth, each with its own language, and the line from Shem rested in a household that had stopped short of Canaan. Abram was in Haran. His father was dead. His wife Sarai had no child.

title: The Call of Abraham
subtitle: Genesis 12 to 17, Berean Standard Bible
description: Abram's calling, journeys, promises, Hagar, and the covenant of Abraham and Sarah.
paragraphs: The call came to a man whose family had stopped in Haran.

The LORD said to Abram, "Leave your country, your kindred, and your father's household, and go to the land I will show you. I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you."

Abram went, as the LORD had told him. He was seventy-five years old when he left Haran. He took Sarai his wife, Lot his brother's son, all the possessions they had gathered, and the people they had acquired in Haran. They set out for the land of Canaan, and they arrived there.

The land was not empty. The Canaanites were in the land. Abram traveled through it to the site of Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. There the LORD appeared to Abram and promised the land to his offspring. Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him. He moved to the hill country east of Bethel, pitched his tent with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east, built another altar, and called on the name of the LORD.

Then famine pressed the land. Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while, because the famine was severe. Before they entered Egypt, Abram asked Sarai to say she was his sister. He knew her beauty could put his life in danger. Pharaoh's officials saw Sarai, praised her to Pharaoh, and she was taken into Pharaoh's house. Abram was treated well because of her and gained sheep, cattle, donkeys, servants, and camels.

The LORD struck Pharaoh and his household with serious diseases because of Sarai, Abram's wife. Pharaoh sent for Abram, confronted him for the lie, and gave Sarai back. Pharaoh ordered his men to send Abram away with his wife and everything he had.

Back in the Negev, the promise had a practical problem. Abram was wealthy in livestock, silver, and gold. Lot also had flocks, herds, and tents. The land could not support them while they stayed together, and quarrels broke out between Abram's herdsmen and Lot's herdsmen. Abram let Lot choose first. Lot looked toward the plain of the Jordan, saw that it was well watered everywhere, like the garden of the LORD and like Egypt, and chose it. He moved his tents as far as Sodom. The men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD.

After Lot separated, the LORD told Abram to lift his eyes north, south, east, and west. All the land he saw would be given to him and his offspring forever. His offspring would be like the dust of the earth. Abram moved his tent to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and built an altar there.

Word soon came that war had swept the Jordan plain. Kings had raided Sodom and Gomorrah and carried off Lot and his possessions. A man who escaped told Abram the Hebrew. Abram brought out 318 trained men born in his household and pursued the raiders as far as Dan. At night he divided his forces, attacked, and recovered Lot, the women, the people, and the goods.

On the way back, Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brought out bread and wine and blessed Abram. Abram gave him a tenth of everything. The king of Sodom offered Abram the goods if Abram would give him the people. Abram refused to take so much as a thread or a sandal strap from the king of Sodom. He would not let that king say he had made Abram rich.

After these things, the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision. God told him not to fear. God was his shield and his very great reward. Abram answered with the fact that had followed him from Haran. He remained childless. A servant in his house, Eliezer of Damascus, stood to be his heir.
God took Abram outside and told him to count the stars if he could. So would his offspring be.
"Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness."

God told Abram to bring animals for a covenant: a heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon. Abram cut the animals in two and laid the pieces opposite each other. Birds of prey came down, and Abram drove them away. As the sun set, a deep sleep fell on Abram, and a thick and dreadful darkness came over him. In that darkness God told him his descendants would be strangers in a land not their own, enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years. God would punish the nation they served, and afterward they would come out with great possessions. In the fourth generation they would return to Canaan, because the sin of the Amorites had not yet reached its full measure.
When darkness had fallen, a smoking firepot and a blazing torch passed between the pieces. On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram and named the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.

Years passed. Sarai still had no child. She gave Abram her Egyptian slave Hagar and told him to sleep with her, so that Sarai might build a family through her. Abram listened. Hagar conceived, and when she knew she was pregnant, she began to despise her mistress. Sarai blamed Abram. Abram put Hagar back under Sarai's authority, and Sarai treated her harshly until Hagar fled into the wilderness.

The angel of the LORD found Hagar near a spring. He sent her back to Sarai and told her the child would be a son named Ishmael, because the LORD had heard her misery. Ishmael would be a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone and everyone's hand against him. Hagar bore Abram a son. Abram was eighty-six years old.

Thirteen years later, when Abram was ninety-nine, the LORD appeared to him as God Almighty. The covenant came with a new name. "No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations."

God gave circumcision as the sign of the covenant. Every male in Abraham's household was to be circumcised, including those born in his house and those bought with money. Sarai received a new name too. She would be Sarah, and God would bless her and give Abraham a son by her. Kings of peoples would come from her.

Abraham fell facedown and laughed. A son born to a man one hundred years old and to Sarah at ninety sounded impossible inside ordinary life. Abraham asked that Ishmael might live before God. God answered that Sarah would bear a son, and Abraham was to name him Isaac. God would establish His covenant with Isaac. Ishmael would also be blessed and made into a great nation, but the covenant would stand with Isaac, whom Sarah would bear at the appointed time next year.
That very day Abraham took Ishmael and every male in his household and circumcised them, as God had told him.
Abraham had a new name. Sarah had a new name. Isaac had a name before he had been conceived.

title: Sodom, Isaac, and the Mountain
subtitle: Genesis 18 to 22, Berean Standard Bible
description: Abraham and Sarah, Sodom, the birth of Isaac, and the difficult test at Moriah.
paragraphs: The LORD appeared to Abraham near the oaks of Mamre while Abraham sat at the entrance to his tent in the heat of the day.

Abraham looked up and saw three men standing nearby. He ran to meet them, bowed low, and pressed them to stay. Water was brought to wash their feet. Abraham hurried into the tent and told Sarah to make bread from fine flour. He ran to the herd, chose a tender calf, and gave it to a servant to prepare. Then he set curds, milk, and the calf before the men under the tree, and he stood near them while they ate.
One of them said Sarah would have a son.

Sarah was listening at the tent entrance behind him. Abraham and Sarah were old, well along in years, and Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. She laughed to herself. The LORD asked Abraham why Sarah laughed and said, "Is anything too difficult for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, in about a year, and Sarah will have a son."
Sarah denied laughing because she was afraid. The answer stayed firm. She had laughed.

Then the men looked toward Sodom, and Abraham walked with them to send them on their way. What followed turned Abraham from host to intercessor. The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah was great, and their sin was very grave. The LORD would go down and see.

Abraham remained standing before the LORD. He drew near and asked whether God would sweep away the righteous with the wicked. If fifty righteous people were in the city, would God spare the whole place for their sake? Abraham said, "Far be it from You to do such a thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous and the wicked are treated alike. Far be it from You! Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?"

The number moved downward as Abraham kept asking. Fifty. Forty-five. Forty. Thirty. Twenty. Ten. Each time, God answered that the city would be spared for the sake of the righteous found there. Abraham knew he was dust and ashes, and he kept speaking anyway.

By evening, two angels came to Sodom. Lot sat at the gate. He bowed, urged them to spend the night in his house, washed their feet, and prepared a meal. Before they had gone to bed, the men of Sodom surrounded the house, from young to old, and demanded that Lot bring out his guests so they could have relations with them.

Lot went outside and shut the door behind him. He begged the men not to do this wicked thing. Then he made an offer that exposes how broken the city had become. He offered his two virgin daughters to the crowd instead. The men rejected him, accused him of judging them though he had come to Sodom as a foreigner, and pressed hard against the door.

The angels pulled Lot back inside and struck the men outside with blindness, so they could not find the doorway. Then they told Lot to gather everyone who belonged to him and leave. The city was about to be destroyed.

Lot went to his sons-in-law and urged them to get up and leave, but they thought he was joking. At dawn the angels urged Lot to hurry. He hesitated. The angels seized his hand, his wife's hand, and the hands of his two daughters, because the LORD was merciful to him, and brought them outside the city. They told the family to flee for their lives, not to look back, and not to stop anywhere in the plain. Lot feared the mountains and asked to flee to a small town nearby. The town was called Zoar.

By the time Lot reached Zoar, the sun had risen. Then the LORD rained down brimstone and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, out of the heavens. He overthrew those cities, the whole plain, all who lived in the cities, and what grew on the ground. Lot's wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.

Early the next morning Abraham went to the place where he had stood before the LORD. He looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and saw dense smoke rising from the land, like smoke from a furnace. God had remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the destruction.

Lot left Zoar and lived in the mountains with his two daughters because he was afraid to stay in Zoar. In a cave, the older daughter said their father was old and there was no man in the land to give them children. On two nights they made Lot drink wine until he did not know what was happening, and each daughter slept with him. The older daughter bore Moab. The younger bore Ben-Ammi. Genesis gives their names as fathers of the Moabites and the Ammonites.

Later Abraham moved between Kadesh and Shur and lived in Gerar. There he repeated the old fear. He said Sarah was his sister. Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for Sarah and took her. God came to Abimelech in a dream and warned him that he was as good as dead because Sarah was a married woman. Abimelech pleaded that he had acted with a clear conscience and clean hands because Abraham and Sarah both had said they were brother and sister.

God kept Abimelech from sinning against Him with Sarah and told him to return her to Abraham, who was a prophet and would pray for him. Early in the morning Abimelech told his officials the dream. They were afraid. He confronted Abraham for deceiving him and risking guilt on the kingdom. Abraham answered that he had feared there was no fear of God in that place and that he would be killed because of his wife. Sarah truly was his half-sister, and Abraham had asked her to show him kindness by calling him her brother wherever they went.

Abimelech restored Sarah, gave Abraham sheep, cattle, and servants, and gave Sarah a thousand pieces of silver. He told Abraham his land lay before him. Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants so they could bear children again, for the LORD had closed every womb in Abimelech's household because of Sarah.

Then the appointed time reached Sarah. The LORD was gracious to her as He had said, and Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the very time God had promised. Abraham named him Isaac. When Isaac was eight days old, Abraham circumcised him, as God had commanded. Abraham was one hundred years old when Isaac was born.
Sarah said God had brought her laughter, and everyone who heard would laugh with her. The child grew and was weaned. Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned.

Sarah saw Ishmael, the son Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham, mocking. She told Abraham to drive out the slave woman and her son, because Ishmael would not share Isaac's inheritance. The matter distressed Abraham greatly because it concerned his son. God told Abraham not to be distressed. He was to listen to Sarah, because through Isaac his offspring would be reckoned. God would also make Ishmael into a nation because he was Abraham's offspring.

Early the next morning Abraham gave Hagar bread and a skin of water, put them on her shoulder, and sent her away with the boy. She wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. When the water was gone, she put the boy under a bush and sat down at a distance. She could not watch him die. As she wept, God heard the boy crying. The angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and told her not to be afraid. God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She filled the skin and gave the boy a drink.
God was with the boy as he grew up. Ishmael lived in the wilderness and became an archer. His mother got a wife for him from Egypt.

At Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his forces, made a treaty with Abraham. They recognized that God was with Abraham in everything he did. Abraham raised a complaint about a well his servants had seized. Abimelech said he had not known. Abraham gave sheep and cattle, and he set apart seven ewe lambs as a witness that he had dug the well. The place was called Beersheba, because there the two men swore an oath. Abraham planted a tamarisk tree there and called on the name of the LORD, the Eternal God.
Some time later God tested Abraham.

He told Abraham to take Isaac, his only son, whom he loved, and go to the land of Moriah. There Abraham was to offer Isaac as a burnt offering on one of the mountains God would name. Early the next morning Abraham saddled his donkey, split wood for the offering, took two servants and Isaac, and set out.

On the third day Abraham lifted his eyes and saw the place in the distance. He told the servants to stay with the donkey. He and Isaac would worship and then return. Abraham took the wood, laid it on Isaac, and carried the fire and the knife himself. As they walked together, Isaac asked about the lamb for the burnt offering. Abraham answered, "God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son." And the two walked on together.

When they reached the place God had told him about, Abraham built an altar, arranged the wood, bound Isaac, and laid him on the altar on top of the wood. Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.

The angel of the LORD called from heaven and told him to stop. "Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him," said the angel, "for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me."
Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering instead of his son. Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide.

The angel called a second time and confirmed the promise because Abraham had obeyed. His descendants would be as many as the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore. They would take possession of the gates of their enemies, and through Abraham's offspring all nations on earth would be blessed.

Abraham returned to his servants, and they went together to Beersheba. After this, Abraham received news from his brother Nahor's family in the north. Among the names was Bethuel, and Bethuel had become the father of Rebekah.

title: A Wife for Isaac and Two Twin Brothers
subtitle: Genesis 23 to 27, Berean Standard Bible
description: Sarah's burial, Rebekah and Isaac, Esau and Jacob, and a blessing gained by deceit.
paragraphs: Sarah died in Hebron, and Abraham's first piece of the promised land was a grave.

Sarah lived 127 years. She died at Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Abraham went to mourn for her and to weep over her. Then he rose from beside his dead wife and spoke to the Hittites who lived there. He was a foreigner and stranger among them, and he asked for a burial site so he could bury his dead.

The Hittites called Abraham a mighty prince among them and offered him the finest of their tombs. Abraham bowed and asked them to speak to Ephron son of Zohar for the cave of Machpelah at the end of Ephron's field. Abraham did not want the cave as a favor. He wanted to buy the field for the full price and hold it as his own burial property.

Ephron answered in the hearing of the people and named the whole field, the cave, and the trees within its borders. Abraham weighed out the price in the hearing of the Hittites: 400 shekels of silver, according to the standard of the merchants. The field passed to Abraham as his property in the sight of all who entered the gate of the city. Abraham buried Sarah in the cave of the field of Machpelah near Mamre, at Hebron in the land of Canaan.
The promise had named a whole land. Abraham now owned a field, a cave, and the place where Sarah lay.

By then Abraham was old and well advanced in years, and the LORD had blessed him in every way. He called the oldest servant in his household, the man in charge of all he had, and made him swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and earth. The servant was not to take a wife for Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom Abraham lived. He was to go to Abraham's country and kindred and get a wife for Isaac there.

The servant asked the hard question. What if the woman was unwilling to come back with him? Should he take Isaac to the land Abraham had left? Abraham said no. Isaac must not go back there. The God who had taken Abraham from his father's house would send His angel before the servant. If the woman was unwilling, the servant would be released from the oath.

The servant took ten of Abraham's camels and departed with gifts for Aram Naharaim, to the city of Nahor. He made the camels kneel by the well outside the city toward evening, when women went out to draw water. There he prayed for a sign specific enough to trust. The woman who offered him a drink and also offered to draw water for his camels would be the one the LORD had appointed for Isaac.

Before he had finished praying, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder. She was the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Milcah and Nahor, Abraham's brother. She filled her jar, offered the servant a drink, and then drew water for all his camels until they had finished drinking. The servant watched her in silence, waiting to learn whether the LORD had made his journey successful.

When the camels had finished, he gave her a gold ring and two gold bracelets and asked whose daughter she was. He asked whether there was room in her father's house for him to spend the night. Rebekah answered and ran to tell her mother's household. Her brother Laban saw the jewelry and heard her words. He came out to the servant by the spring and brought him into the house.

Food was set before the servant, but he would not eat until he had told his errand. He named Abraham, named Isaac, and told how he had prayed at the well before Rebekah came. Bethuel and Laban answered that the matter had come from the LORD and could not be spoken against. Rebekah stood before the servant. He could take her and go, so she could become the wife of Abraham's son.
They called Rebekah and asked her, "Will you go with this man?" "I will go," she replied.

Her family blessed her and sent her away with the servant. In the Negev, Isaac had come from Beer Lahai Roi and was living in the land of the south. Toward evening he went out to the field to meditate and lifted his eyes. Camels were coming. Rebekah lifted her eyes too, saw Isaac, and slipped down from the camel. When she learned who he was, she took her veil and covered herself.
The servant told Isaac everything he had done. "And Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah and took Rebekah as his wife. And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother's death."

Abraham took another wife, Keturah, and she bore him sons. Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them eastward, away from Isaac, while he was still living. He gave everything he owned to Isaac. Abraham lived 175 years. He breathed his last and died at a good old age, an old man and full of years, and he was gathered to his people. Isaac and Ishmael buried him with Sarah in the cave of Machpelah.
Ishmael's line is named, twelve princes according to their tribes, and Ishmael died at 137.

Isaac's own family began with a familiar grief. Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of Rebekah because she was barren. The LORD answered, and Rebekah conceived. The children struggled together inside her. She asked why this was happening to her and went to inquire of the LORD.
The LORD declared to her: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you will be separated; one people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger."

When the days to give birth came, there were twins in her womb. The first came out red, covered with hair like a garment, and they named him Esau. Afterward his brother came out with his hand gripping Esau's heel, so he was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when the twins were born.

The boys grew up with different shapes to their lives. Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the open country. Jacob was a quiet man, staying among the tents. Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his game. Rebekah loved Jacob.

Once Jacob was cooking stew when Esau came in from the field famished. Esau asked for some of the red stew because he was exhausted. Jacob answered that Esau must first sell him his birthright. Esau said he was about to die, and asked what good the birthright was to him. Jacob made him swear. Esau swore and sold his birthright for bread and lentil stew. He ate, drank, rose, and went away. Genesis says, "Thus Esau despised his birthright."

A famine came in the days of Isaac, separate from the famine in Abraham's days. Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerar. The LORD appeared to Isaac and told him not to go down to Egypt. He was to live in the land God told him about. God repeated the promise of land, offspring, and blessing to the nations. Isaac stayed in Gerar.

In Gerar, Isaac used Abraham's old fear. When the men of the place asked about Rebekah, he said she was his sister because he feared he might die on account of her. After Isaac had been there a long time, Abimelech looked down from a window and saw Isaac caressing Rebekah. The king called Isaac and confronted him. A man of the people might have slept with Rebekah and brought guilt on them. Isaac admitted he had feared for his life. Abimelech ordered all the people not to touch Isaac or his wife, on pain of death.

Isaac planted crops in that land and reaped a hundredfold in the same year because the LORD blessed him. He became rich and kept gaining wealth until he was very wealthy. He had flocks, herds, and many servants, and the Philistines envied him. They filled with earth the wells Abraham's servants had dug. Abimelech told Isaac to move away because he had become too powerful.

Isaac dug again in the valley. His herdsmen quarreled with Gerar's herdsmen over water. One well was named Esek, because they disputed it. Another was named Sitnah, because they accused him. Then Isaac moved and dug another well. No one quarreled over it, so he named it Rehoboth, because the LORD had made room for them to flourish in the land.

From there Isaac went up to Beersheba. That night the LORD appeared to him and repeated the promise as the God of Abraham. Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD. His servants dug a well. Abimelech came from Gerar with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his forces. When Isaac asked why they had come after hating him and sending him away, they replied, "We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you." They made a covenant and feasted. Isaac sent them away in peace. That same day Isaac's servants told him about water they had found.
When Esau was forty years old, he married Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite. They made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.

Isaac was old, and his eyes were so dim he could not see. He called Esau and told him to take his weapons, hunt game, prepare the tasty food Isaac loved, and bring it to him so Isaac could bless Esau before he died. Rebekah was listening. When Esau went to the field, Rebekah spoke to Jacob. She had heard Isaac's words, and she had a plan to place Jacob in front of them. Jacob was to bring two young goats. Rebekah would prepare the food Isaac loved. Jacob would carry it to his father, who might bless Jacob before his death.

Jacob raised the obvious problem. Esau was hairy, and he was smooth. If Isaac touched him, Jacob would seem like a trickster and bring a curse instead of a blessing. Rebekah answered that the curse would fall on her. She told Jacob to obey her voice.

Jacob brought the goats. Rebekah cooked the food, put Esau's best clothes on Jacob, and covered his hands and the smooth part of his neck with goat skins. Then she placed the food and bread in Jacob's hands.

Jacob went to his father and said he was Esau, his firstborn. Isaac asked how the game had been found so quickly. Jacob said the LORD his God had granted him success. Isaac told him to come near so he could feel whether Jacob was really Esau. The voice was Jacob's voice, but the hands were the hands of Esau. Isaac ate, drank wine, drew Jacob near, and kissed him. He smelled the clothing, the smell of a field the LORD had blessed, and spoke the blessing.

"May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you. May you be the master of your brothers, and may the sons of your mother bow down to you. May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed."

Jacob had scarcely left when Esau came in from hunting. He prepared food and brought it to his father. Isaac trembled violently when he learned who had come before him. The blessing spoken over Jacob would stand. Esau cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and begged his father to bless him too. Isaac answered that Jacob had come with deceit and taken Esau's blessing.

Esau still received words from his father about living by the sword and serving his brother, and about a time when he would grow restless and break Jacob's yoke from his neck. The words did not cool his anger. Esau hated Jacob and planned to kill him after the days of mourning for Isaac.

Rebekah heard Esau's plan. She sent Jacob away to Laban, her brother in Haran, until Esau's fury turned aside. To Isaac, she spoke of her weariness with the Hittite women Esau had married. If Jacob married one of them, she said her life would be worth nothing. Isaac called Jacob, blessed him, charged him not to take a wife from the Canaanite women, and sent him to Paddan-aram to take a wife from the daughters of Laban.
Jacob obeyed his father and mother. He left Beersheba and went toward Haran, carrying a stolen blessing and a father's command.

title: Jacob Runs, Dreams, and Wrestles
subtitle: Genesis 28 to 33, Berean Standard Bible
description: Jacob's journey to Haran, his growing family, a night of wrestling, and reunion with Esau.
paragraphs: Jacob left home with Esau behind him and Haran ahead of him, and the first night found him sleeping under open sky.

He came to a certain place and stopped for the night because the sun had set. He took one of the stones from that place, put it under his head, and lay down to sleep. Then Jacob dreamed. A stairway rested on the earth, and its top reached to heaven. The angels of God were ascending and descending on it. The LORD stood above it and spoke the promise Jacob had taken by deceit, only now God gave it directly to Jacob.

God promised the land on which Jacob lay to Jacob and his offspring. His offspring would be like the dust of the earth and would spread out to the west, east, north, and south. In Jacob and in his seed all the families of the earth would be blessed. Then God spoke to the runaway himself. "Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you."

Jacob woke and knew the place had changed for him. He had thought he was alone on the road, and he said the LORD was in that place and he had not known it. He was afraid. He called the place the house of God and the gate of heaven. Early in the morning he took the stone that had been under his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on top of it. He named the place Bethel, though the city had been called Luz. Jacob made a vow. If God would be with him, watch over him, give him food and clothing, and bring him back in peace to his father's house, then the LORD would be his God. The stone pillar would be God's house, and Jacob would give God a tenth of all God gave him.

Jacob continued on his journey and came to the land of the people of the east. A well stood in the field with a large stone over its mouth. Flocks gathered there, but shepherds waited until all the flocks came before rolling the stone away. Jacob asked the shepherds where they were from. They said Haran. They knew Laban, the grandson of Nahor, and they pointed to Rachel, Laban's daughter, coming with the sheep.

While Jacob was still speaking with them, Rachel arrived with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess. Jacob went up and rolled the stone from the mouth of the well and watered his uncle Laban's flock. Then Jacob kissed Rachel and began to weep aloud. He told her he was her father's relative, Rebekah's son. Rachel ran and told her father.

Laban hurried out to meet Jacob, embraced him, kissed him, and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all that had happened. After Jacob had stayed with him a full month, Laban told him he should not serve for nothing just because he was a relative. Jacob was to name his wages.

Laban had two daughters. Leah was the older. Rachel was younger, lovely in form and beautiful. Jacob loved Rachel, and he offered to serve Laban seven years for her. Laban agreed that it was better to give Rachel to Jacob than to another man. Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed like a few days to him because of the love he had for her.

When the seven years were complete, Jacob asked Laban to give him his wife. Laban gathered all the men of the place and made a feast. In the evening he took Leah his daughter and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob went in to her. Laban gave his servant Zilpah to Leah as her maidservant. In the morning, Jacob discovered it was Leah.

Jacob confronted Laban for deceiving him. He had served for Rachel. Laban answered that in their country the younger daughter was not given before the firstborn. Jacob was to finish Leah's bridal week, and then Rachel would also be given to him if he served another seven years. Jacob did so. Laban gave Rachel to him as wife, with Bilhah as her maidservant, and Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.

When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb, while Rachel remained barren. Leah bore a son and named him Reuben, because the LORD had looked on her affliction. She conceived again and bore Simeon. She conceived again and bore Levi. She conceived again and bore Judah, saying this time she would praise the LORD. Then she stopped bearing children for a time.

Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, and she envied her sister. She told Jacob to give her children, or she would die. Jacob's anger burned against Rachel, and he answered that he was not in the place of God, who had withheld children from her. Rachel gave him Bilhah, her servant, so Bilhah could bear children on Rachel's behalf and Rachel could build a family through her. Bilhah bore Jacob a son, and Rachel named him Dan, saying God had vindicated her. Bilhah bore a second son, and Rachel named him Naphtali.

Leah saw that she had stopped bearing, so she gave Zilpah, her servant, to Jacob. Zilpah bore Gad. Zilpah bore a second son, Asher. During the wheat harvest, Reuben found mandrakes in the field and brought them to Leah. Rachel asked Leah for some of the mandrakes. Leah answered that Rachel had taken her husband, and now she wanted her son's mandrakes too. Rachel offered Jacob to Leah for that night in return. Leah met Jacob when he came in from the field and told him he must come to her, because she had hired him with the mandrakes. God listened to Leah. She bore Issachar. She bore Zebulun. Afterward she bore a daughter, Dinah.

Then God remembered Rachel. God listened to her and opened her womb. She conceived and bore a son, Joseph. Rachel said God had taken away her disgrace, and she named him Joseph, saying the LORD would add another son to her.

After Rachel had borne Joseph, Jacob asked Laban to send him away to his own place and country. He had served for his wives and children, and Laban knew the service Jacob had given him. Laban asked him to stay. He had learned that the LORD blessed him because of Jacob. They set new wages. Jacob would take every speckled and spotted sheep, every dark lamb, and every spotted goat as his pay. Laban agreed, but that same day he removed the striped and spotted male goats, the speckled and spotted female goats, and the dark lambs, and put them in the care of his sons. He put a three-day journey between himself and Jacob.

Jacob still prospered. Genesis says he took fresh rods from poplar, almond, and plane trees, peeled white stripes in them, and set the rods in the watering troughs where the flocks came to drink and mate. The flocks bore striped, speckled, and spotted young. Jacob separated the animals and used the stronger flocks for his plan, while Laban's weaker animals stayed Laban's. Jacob grew exceedingly prosperous and came to own many flocks, female and male servants, camels, and donkeys.

Then Jacob heard the words of Laban's sons, who said Jacob had taken all that belonged to their father and gained his wealth from it. Jacob saw that Laban's attitude toward him had changed. The LORD told Jacob to return to the land of his fathers and to his relatives, and God would be with him.

Jacob sent for Rachel and Leah in the field where his flock was. He told them their father's attitude had changed, but the God of his father had been with him. He told them Laban had cheated him and changed his wages ten times, yet God had not allowed Laban to harm him. In a dream during breeding season, the angel of God had shown Jacob that the rams were striped, speckled, and mottled, and had called Jacob to leave: "I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the pillar and made a solemn vow to Me. Now get up, leave this land at once, and return to your native land."

Rachel and Leah answered that their father had treated them like foreigners. He had sold them and used up what was paid for them. All the wealth God had taken from Laban belonged to Jacob and their children. They told Jacob to do all God had said.

Jacob put his children and wives on camels and drove all his livestock ahead of him, all the property he had accumulated in Paddan-aram, to go to Isaac his father in Canaan. While Laban had gone to shear his sheep, Rachel stole her father's household gods. Jacob deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him he was fleeing. They crossed the Euphrates and set out for the hill country of Gilead.

Laban learned of the flight on the third day and pursued with his relatives. After seven days he caught up with Jacob in Gilead. But God came to Laban in a dream by night and warned him not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.

Laban confronted Jacob for leaving secretly, carrying away his daughters like captives taken in war, and stealing his gods. Jacob answered the charge of flight with fear. He had been afraid Laban would take his daughters by force. As for the gods, Jacob said whoever was found with them should not live, unaware that Rachel had taken them. Laban searched Jacob's tent, Leah's tent, and the tents of the two maidservants. He came to Rachel's tent. Rachel had put the household gods in the camel's saddle and sat on them. She told her father she could not rise before him because the way of women was upon her. Laban searched and did not find them.

Jacob's anger burned. He recounted twenty years under Laban: fourteen years for Laban's two daughters and six years for his flock. His wages had been changed ten times. Jacob had borne the loss of animals torn by beasts. In the day heat consumed him, and in the night the frost, and sleep fled from his eyes. If the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac had not been with Jacob, Laban would have sent him away empty-handed.

Laban claimed the daughters, children, and flocks were his, yet he proposed a covenant so he would not harm Jacob and Jacob would not harm him. Jacob set up a stone pillar. The heap and pillar were named witness between them. The place was called Mizpah, because Laban said the LORD would watch between them while they were absent from one another. Early the next morning Laban kissed his grandchildren and daughters, blessed them, and returned home.

Jacob went on his way, and angels of God met him. He called the place Mahanaim, two camps. From there he sent messengers ahead to his brother Esau, in the land of Seir, the country of Edom. The messengers returned with a report that tightened Jacob's whole body around the old danger. Esau was coming to meet Jacob, and four hundred men were with him.

Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed. He divided the people with him, the flocks, herds, and camels, into two camps. If Esau attacked one camp, the other might escape. Then Jacob prayed. He called on the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac. He reminded God of the command to return and of the promise that his offspring would be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted. Jacob said he was unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness God had shown him. With only his staff he had crossed the Jordan, and now he had become two camps. He asked God to deliver him from the hand of Esau.

That night Jacob prepared a gift for his brother: goats, sheep, camels, cows, bulls, and donkeys, arranged in droves with space between them. Servants went ahead in waves. Each servant was to tell Esau the animals were a gift from his servant Jacob and that Jacob was coming behind them. Jacob hoped to pacify Esau with the gift going before him, and afterward see his face. Perhaps Esau would accept him.
Jacob sent his family over the ford of the Jabbok and remained alone on the other side.

A man wrestled with Jacob until the breaking of the day. When the man saw that he did not prevail against Jacob, he touched Jacob's hip socket, and Jacob's hip was put out of joint as he wrestled. The man asked to be released because the day was breaking. Jacob answered that he would not let go unless he was blessed.
The man asked Jacob's name, and Jacob gave it. Then the man said, "Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed."

Jacob asked for the man's name, but the man asked why Jacob asked and blessed him there. Jacob called the place Peniel, because he had seen God face to face, and yet his life had been preserved. The sun rose above him as he passed Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip. Genesis adds that to this day the Israelites do not eat the tendon of the hip socket, because the man touched Jacob's hip socket there.

Jacob lifted his eyes and saw Esau coming with his four hundred men. He divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two maidservants. He placed the maidservants and their children in front, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph last. Jacob himself went on ahead and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother.
"Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept."

Esau asked about the women and children. Jacob answered that they were the children God had graciously given his servant. The maidservants and their children approached and bowed down. Leah and her children approached and bowed down. Joseph and Rachel approached and bowed down. Esau asked about the droves he had met. Jacob said they were to find favor in Esau's sight. Esau said he already had plenty and told Jacob to keep what was his. Jacob urged him to accept, saying he had seen Esau's face as one sees the face of God, and Esau had received him favorably. Esau accepted the gift.

Esau offered to journey with Jacob or leave men with him. Jacob pointed to the children and the nursing flocks and herds. If they were driven hard for one day, the flocks would die. Esau should go ahead to Seir, and Jacob would lead on slowly, at the pace of the children and the livestock. Esau returned that day on his way to Seir. Jacob journeyed to Succoth, where he built a house for himself and booths for his livestock.

Then Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan. He camped within sight of the city and bought the plot of land where he had pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, for one hundred pieces of silver. There he erected an altar and called it El Elohe Israel.
Jacob was back in the land his grandfather had bought only as a burial field. This time he bought ground for his living household and set an altar on it.

title: A Family Breaking Apart
subtitle: Genesis 34 to 38, Berean Standard Bible
description: Dinah, the losses in Jacob's family, Joseph's betrayal, and the account of Judah and Tamar.
paragraphs: Dinah went out, and what happened to her split her brothers open.

Dinah was the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob. She went out to see the women of the land. Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite and a prince of the land, saw her. He took her and lay with her by force. His soul was drawn to Dinah, and he loved her and spoke tenderly to her after he had violated her. Shechem told his father Hamor to get the girl for him as a wife.
When Jacob heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah, his sons were in the field with his livestock. Jacob kept silent until they came home.

Hamor went out to speak with Jacob. At the same time Jacob's sons came in from the field. When they heard what had happened, the men were grieved and furious, "because Shechem had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter, a thing that should not be done."

Hamor asked for Dinah as a wife for Shechem and offered open doors between their peoples. Their daughters could marry each other's sons. They could live in the land together, trade in it, and acquire property. Shechem added his own plea. He would give whatever bride price and gift they asked, if only they would give him the girl to be his wife.

Jacob's sons answered Shechem and Hamor with deceit because Shechem had defiled Dinah. They said they could not give their sister to a man who was uncircumcised. The men of the city could become one people with them if every male among them was circumcised as Jacob's household was. Hamor and Shechem carried the proposal to the men at the city gate. They framed it as peace and profit: the people's land, livestock, and property could belong to Shechem's city if the men agreed. Every male was circumcised.

On the third day, while the men were still in pain, Dinah's brothers Simeon and Levi took their swords, came against the unsuspecting city, and killed every male. They killed Hamor and Shechem with the sword, took Dinah from Shechem's house, and departed. The other sons of Jacob came upon the dead and plundered the city because their sister had been defiled. They took flocks, herds, donkeys, wealth, children, wives, and everything in the houses and fields.

Jacob said to Simeon and Levi that they had brought trouble on him by making him a stench to the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. Jacob's household was small in number. If the peoples gathered against him, they could destroy him and his household. Simeon and Levi answered with the wound the story would not put down. Should Shechem have treated their sister like a prostitute?

Then God told Jacob to arise, go up to Bethel, and live there. Jacob was to make an altar to the God who had appeared to him when he fled from Esau. Jacob ordered his household and all who were with him to put away the foreign gods among them, purify themselves, and change their garments. They gave Jacob all the foreign gods in their possession and the rings in their ears, and Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem.

As they journeyed, the terror of God fell on the cities around them, and no one pursued Jacob's sons. Jacob came to Luz, which is Bethel, in the land of Canaan. He built an altar and called the place El Bethel, because there God had revealed Himself to Jacob when he fled from his brother. Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died and was buried under the oak below Bethel. It was named Allon-bachuth, Oak of Weeping.

God appeared to Jacob again after he came from Paddan-aram and blessed him. God repeated the name change: Jacob would no longer be called Jacob, but Israel would be his name. God said, "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply." He promised that nations and kings would come from Jacob, and He gave Jacob the land He had given to Abraham and Isaac. Jacob set up a stone pillar where God had spoken with him and poured out a drink offering and oil on it. He called the place Bethel.

They journeyed from Bethel, and while they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel went into labor. Her labor was hard. The midwife told her not to fear, because she would have another son. As Rachel's soul was departing, for she was dying, she named the boy Ben-oni, Son of My Sorrow. His father called him Benjamin. Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Jacob set a pillar over her tomb.
While Israel lived in that region, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard of it.

Genesis then names Jacob's twelve sons. Leah bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. Rachel bore Joseph and Benjamin. Bilhah, Rachel's servant, bore Dan and Naphtali. Zilpah, Leah's servant, bore Gad and Asher. Jacob came to Isaac at Mamre, at Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had lived as foreigners. Isaac lived 180 years. He breathed his last and died, old and full of days, and Esau and Jacob buried him.

Esau's family receives its own record. Esau had taken wives from Canaan, and he had sons who became chiefs in Edom. He moved from the land of Canaan because the land could not support both his household and Jacob's household with all their livestock. Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Genesis names his descendants, the chiefs of the sons of Esau, and kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel. Jacob's twin had become a nation with its own rulers.
Joseph enters the next movement at seventeen years old.

Joseph was tending the flock with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father's wives, and he brought a bad report about them to their father. Israel loved Joseph more than any of his other sons because he had been born to him in his old age. Israel made Joseph a robe of many colors. "When Joseph's brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him."

Joseph had a dream. In the dream, he and his brothers were binding sheaves in the field. Joseph's sheaf rose and stood upright, and his brothers' sheaves gathered around it and bowed down. His brothers asked whether he intended to reign over them or rule over them, and they hated him even more. Then Joseph dreamed another dream. The sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to him. He told his father and his brothers. Israel rebuked him and asked whether he, Joseph's mother, and Joseph's brothers would actually come and bow to the ground before Joseph. His brothers were jealous of him, "but his father kept in mind what he had said."

Israel sent Joseph from the Valley of Hebron to see if all was well with his brothers and the flock at Shechem. Joseph found a man wandering in the field near Shechem, and the man told him the brothers had moved on to Dothan. Joseph went after them.

His brothers saw him in the distance, and before he reached them they plotted to kill him. They spoke of throwing him into a pit and blaming a fierce animal. Reuben heard the plan and tried to rescue Joseph. He told them not to shed blood, but to throw Joseph into a pit in the wilderness and not lay a hand on him. Reuben meant to return later, pull Joseph out, and bring him back to their father.

When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of the robe Israel had made for him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty. There was no water in it. As they sat down to eat, they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead with spices, balm, and myrrh, on their way to Egypt. Judah asked what would be gained by killing their brother and concealing his blood. He proposed selling Joseph to the Ishmaelites instead of laying a hand on him, because Joseph was their brother and their own flesh.
"So when the Midianite traders passed by, his brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt."

Reuben returned to the pit and found Joseph gone. He tore his clothes and demanded where he could go now. The brothers took Joseph's robe, slaughtered a goat, and dipped the robe in the blood. They sent it to their father and asked him to identify whether it was his son's robe or not. Jacob recognized it. He said a fierce animal had devoured Joseph, that Joseph had surely been torn to pieces. Jacob tore his garments, put sackcloth around his waist, and mourned for his son many days.
"All his sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. 'No,' he said. 'I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son.' So his father wept for him."
Meanwhile the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and the captain of the guard.

Around that time, Judah went down from his brothers and stayed with a man named Hirah the Adullamite. There Judah married the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua. She bore three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Judah obtained a wife for Er, his firstborn. Her name was Tamar. Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.

Judah told Onan to go in to his brother's wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Onan knew the offspring would not be his, so whenever he went in to Tamar he wasted his seed on the ground so he would not give offspring to his brother. What he did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death too. Judah told Tamar to live as a widow in her father's house until Shelah grew up. He said that in words, but he feared Shelah might die like his brothers. He did not give Shelah to Tamar.

After a long time, Judah's wife died. When Judah had finished mourning, he went up to Timnah with Hirah to his sheepshearers. Tamar was told that her father-in-law was going up to Timnah. She took off her widow's garments, covered herself with a veil, wrapped herself, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, on the road to Timnah. She had seen that Shelah had grown up, and she had not been given to him as a wife.

Judah saw her and thought she was a prostitute because she had covered her face. He turned aside to her by the road and asked to come in to her. He did not know she was his daughter-in-law. Tamar asked what he would give her. Judah promised a young goat from his flock. Tamar asked for a pledge until he sent it: his signet, his cord, and the staff in his hand. Judah gave them to her and went in to her, and she conceived by him. Then Tamar arose and went away. She laid aside her veil and put her widow's garments back on.

Judah sent the young goat by Hirah to recover the pledge, but Hirah could not find the woman. Men of the place said there had been no prostitute there. Judah let the matter rest so he would not become a laughingstock. About three months later, Judah was told that Tamar had prostituted herself and was pregnant.
