Judah said she should be brought out and burned.

As she was being brought out, Tamar sent a message to her father-in-law. She said she was pregnant by the man to whom the signet, cord, and staff belonged, and asked Judah to identify them. Judah recognized the items and said, "She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah." And he did not have relations with her again.

When the time came for Tamar to give birth, there were twins in her womb. During labor one child put out a hand. The midwife tied a scarlet thread around his hand, saying this one came out first. But the hand drew back, and his brother came out. She said a breach had been made, and he was named Perez. Afterward his brother came out with the scarlet thread on his hand, and he was named Zerah.

The household of Israel was in pieces. Dinah had been violated and avenged with a sword. Rachel was buried on the road. Reuben had shamed his father. Esau's nation stood apart. Jacob believed Joseph was dead. Judah's own house carried twins born from the pledge he had left beside a road.
And Joseph, the son Jacob mourned as dead, was alive in Egypt in the house of Potiphar.

title: Joseph in Egypt
subtitle: Genesis 39 to 41, Berean Standard Bible
description: Joseph's life in Egypt, imprisonment, the dreams, and the plan for famine.
paragraphs: Joseph arrived in Egypt as property, and the house he served began to prosper around him.

The LORD was with Joseph in the house of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and the captain of the guard. "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, serving in the household of his Egyptian master." Potiphar saw that the LORD was with Joseph and that the LORD made everything Joseph did succeed. Joseph found favor in Potiphar's eyes and became his personal attendant. Potiphar put Joseph in charge of his household and entrusted everything he owned to Joseph's care. From that time, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake, in the house and in the field. Potiphar left everything he had in Joseph's care and concerned himself only with the food he ate.

Joseph was handsome in form and appearance. After some time, Potiphar's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and told him to lie with her. Joseph refused. He told her Potiphar had withheld nothing from him except her, because she was Potiphar's wife. Joseph said, "So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?" She spoke to Joseph day after day, but he refused to lie with her or even be with her.

One day Joseph went into the house to do his work, and none of the household servants was inside. Potiphar's wife caught him by his garment and demanded that he lie with her. Joseph left his garment in her hand, ran outside, and fled. She kept the garment and reshaped the event into an accusation. She told the servants that the Hebrew slave had come to insult them and had fled when she screamed. When Potiphar came home, she repeated the story. His anger burned, and he put Joseph into the prison where the king's prisoners were confined.

Joseph's obedience had landed him in a cell. Genesis does not smooth that fact. It says the LORD was with Joseph there too. The LORD showed him kindness and gave him favor in the eyes of the prison warden. The warden put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were in the prison, and Joseph became responsible for everything done there. The warden did not concern himself with anything under Joseph's care, because the LORD was with Joseph and gave him success in whatever he did.

After some time, Pharaoh's chief cupbearer and chief baker offended their master. Pharaoh put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the same prison where Joseph was confined. The captain put Joseph in charge of them, and they remained in custody for some time.

One night both men had dreams, each with its own meaning. In the morning Joseph saw they were dejected and asked why their faces were so sad. They told him they had dreamed dreams and no one could interpret them. Joseph answered that interpretations belong to God and asked them to tell him the dreams.

The chief cupbearer told his dream first. A vine stood before him with three branches. It budded, blossomed, and produced clusters of ripe grapes. Pharaoh's cup was in his hand, and he took the grapes, squeezed them into Pharaoh's cup, and placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand. Joseph said the three branches were three days. Within three days Pharaoh would lift up the cupbearer's head and restore him to his position. He would place Pharaoh's cup in his hand as before. Joseph asked him to remember Joseph when it went well with him, show him kindness, mention him to Pharaoh, and get him out of that house. Joseph had been taken forcibly from the land of the Hebrews, and in Egypt he had done nothing to deserve the pit.

Seeing that the interpretation was favorable, the baker told his dream. Three baskets of bread were on his head. In the top basket were baked goods for Pharaoh, and birds were eating them out of the basket on his head. Joseph said the three baskets were three days. Within three days Pharaoh would lift the baker's head off and hang him on a tree, and the birds would eat his flesh.

On the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, Pharaoh made a feast for all his servants. He lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and restored him to his position, so the cupbearer placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand. He hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had interpreted to them.
"The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him."
Two full years passed.

Pharaoh had a dream and stood by the Nile. Seven cows came up from the river, sleek and fat, and grazed among the reeds. After them seven other cows came up, ugly and thin. The thin cows stood beside the fat cows on the bank and ate them. Pharaoh awoke. He fell asleep again and dreamed of grain. Seven heads of grain, full and good, grew on one stalk. After them seven other heads sprouted, thin and scorched by the east wind. The thin heads swallowed up the full heads. Pharaoh awoke and realized it was a dream. In the morning his mind was troubled. He sent for the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men and told them his dreams, but no one could interpret them.

Then the chief cupbearer finally remembered. He told Pharaoh about his offense, the baker, the prison, and the young Hebrew servant of the captain of the guard who had interpreted their dreams exactly as events happened. Pharaoh sent for Joseph. Joseph was brought quickly out of the dungeon. He shaved, changed his clothes, and came before Pharaoh.
Pharaoh told Joseph he had heard Joseph could interpret a dream. Joseph answered, "I myself cannot do it," and added, "but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer."

Pharaoh told the dreams again. Joseph said the two dreams were one. God had revealed to Pharaoh what He was about to do. The seven good cows and seven good heads were seven years of great abundance across Egypt. The seven thin cows and seven thin heads were seven years of famine that would follow. The famine would be so severe that the abundance would be forgotten in the land. The dream had come in two forms because the matter had been firmly decided by God, and God would do it soon.

Joseph then gave Pharaoh a plan. Pharaoh should look for a discerning and wise man and put him in charge of the land of Egypt. Overseers should collect a fifth of the produce during the seven years of abundance. All the food of those good years should be gathered and stored under Pharaoh's authority in the cities. That food would be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine, so the land would survive.

The proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his officials. Pharaoh asked them, "Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?" He told Joseph that since God had made all this known to him, no one was as discerning and wise as Joseph. Joseph would be over Pharaoh's house, and all Pharaoh's people would submit to Joseph's word. Only in the throne would Pharaoh be greater.

Pharaoh put his signet ring on Joseph's hand, dressed him in fine linen, and put a gold chain around his neck. Joseph rode in Pharaoh's second chariot, with men calling out before him, "Bow the knee!" Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah and gave him Asenath, daughter of Potiphera priest of On, as his wife.
Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He went out from Pharaoh's presence and traveled throughout Egypt.

During the seven years of abundance, the land produced in great plenty. Joseph gathered all the food and stored it in the cities, putting the food of the fields around each city in that city. Joseph stored up so much grain, like the sand of the sea, that he stopped keeping record because it was beyond measure.

Before the years of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph by Asenath. Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh, saying God had made him forget all his trouble and all his father's house. He named the second Ephraim, saying God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction.

The seven years of abundance in Egypt came to an end. The seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all the lands, but in Egypt there was bread. When all the land of Egypt became hungry, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh told them to go to Joseph and do whatever he said.

The famine was spread over all the face of the earth. Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians, for the famine was severe in the land of Egypt. All the earth came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine was severe in all the earth.
Among the lands touched by famine was Canaan, where Joseph's father still lived.

title: The Brothers Bow
subtitle: Genesis 42 to 45, Berean Standard Bible
description: Joseph's brothers return to Egypt, Benjamin is tested, and Joseph reveals himself.
paragraphs: Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, and his sons stood looking at one another while hunger stood in the room.

Jacob told his sons to go down to Egypt and buy grain so they might live and not die. Ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain. Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph's brother, with them. He feared that harm might happen to Benjamin. Israel's sons came among those who came to buy grain, because the famine was in the land of Canaan.
Joseph was the governor of the land and the one who sold grain to all its people. Joseph's brothers came and bowed themselves before him with their faces to the ground.

Joseph saw his brothers and recognized them, but he treated them as strangers and spoke harshly to them. He asked where they had come from. They said they had come from the land of Canaan to buy food. Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed about them. He accused them of being spies who had come to see the vulnerability of the land.

The brothers answered that they were all sons of one man. They were honest men, twelve brothers in all. The youngest was with their father, and one brother was no more. Joseph said their words would be tested. They would not leave Egypt unless their youngest brother came. One brother would be held in custody while the rest carried grain back for their starving households. Then they were to bring the youngest brother to Joseph. Joseph put them all in custody for three days.

On the third day Joseph told them he feared God. If they were honest men, one brother would remain confined while the rest went home with grain. They had to bring back their youngest brother, so their words would be verified and they would not die. The brothers agreed.

Then they spoke to one another while Joseph listened through an interpreter. They did not know Joseph understood them. They said, "Surely we are being punished because of our brother. We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us." Reuben answered that he had told them not to sin against the boy, but they had not listened. Now his blood was being demanded.

Joseph turned away from them and wept. He returned, spoke to them, and took Simeon from them. Simeon was bound before their eyes. Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, to restore every man's silver to his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey.

The brothers loaded their grain on their donkeys and departed. At the place where they spent the night, one brother opened his sack to give his donkey feed and saw his silver in the mouth of the sack. Their hearts sank, and they trembled. They asked what God had done to them.

When they came to Jacob in Canaan, they told him everything. As they emptied their sacks, each man's bundle of silver was in his sack. Jacob and his sons were afraid. Jacob named the losses one by one: Joseph was no more, Simeon was no more, and now they would take Benjamin. All these things were against him. Reuben spoke up and offered to put his own two sons to death if he did not bring Benjamin back. Jacob refused. His son would not go down with them. Joseph's brother was dead, and Benjamin alone was left. If harm happened to Benjamin on the journey, Jacob said they would bring his gray head down to Sheol in sorrow.

The famine remained severe in the land. When the family had eaten the grain brought from Egypt, Jacob told his sons to go again and buy a little food. Judah answered that the man in Egypt had solemnly warned them they would not see his face unless their brother was with them. If Jacob would send Benjamin with them, they would go and buy food. If he would not send him, they would not go.

Israel asked why they had brought trouble on him by telling the man they had another brother. The brothers answered that the man had questioned them closely about themselves and their family. He had asked whether their father was still alive and whether they had another brother. They had answered his questions. They could not know he would demand that they bring their brother down.

Judah took the responsibility Jacob needed to hear. He told his father to send the boy with him. They would arise and go, so the family might live and not die. Judah would be a pledge for Benjamin's safety. If Judah did not bring him back and set him before Jacob, Judah would bear the blame forever. If they had not delayed, they could have gone and returned twice.

Jacob relented. If it had to be this way, they were to take some of the best products of the land in their bags as a gift for the man: balm, honey, spices, myrrh, pistachio nuts, and almonds. They were to take double the silver, including the silver that had been returned in their sacks, in case it had been an oversight. They were to take Benjamin, arise, and go to the man. Jacob prayed that God Almighty would grant them mercy before the man, so he would let Simeon and Benjamin go. As for Jacob, if he was bereaved, he was bereaved.

The men took the gift, double the silver, and Benjamin. In Egypt they stood before Joseph. When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he told the steward of his house to take the men home, slaughter an animal, and prepare a meal, for the men would eat with Joseph at noon. The steward did as Joseph said, but the brothers were afraid because they had been brought to Joseph's house. They suspected the returned silver would be used as a charge against them, to seize them as slaves and take their donkeys.

They approached the steward at the door and explained the silver. On their first journey they had opened their sacks and found each man's silver in full weight. They had brought it back, with more silver to buy food. The steward told them not to be afraid. Their God and the God of their father had given them treasure in their sacks. He had received their silver. Then he brought Simeon out to them, gave them water to wash their feet, and provided feed for their donkeys.

The brothers prepared their gift for Joseph's arrival at noon, because they had heard they would eat there. When Joseph came home, they presented the gift and bowed to the ground before him. Joseph asked about their welfare and about the old father they had spoken of. Was he still alive? They answered that their father was alive and well, and they bowed low in homage. Joseph lifted his eyes and saw Benjamin, his brother, the son of his mother. He asked whether this was their youngest brother. Joseph said that God would be gracious to him.

Then Joseph hurried out, because his compassion grew warm toward his brother. He sought a place to weep, entered his chamber, and wept there. After he washed his face, he came out and controlled himself. Food was served. Joseph was served by himself, the brothers by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with Joseph by themselves, because Egyptians could not eat with Hebrews, an abomination to the Egyptians. The brothers were seated before Joseph in order from the firstborn to the youngest, according to birth order, and they looked at one another in astonishment. Portions were taken from Joseph's table to them, but Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs. They drank and were merry with Joseph.

Joseph commanded his steward to fill the men's sacks with as much food as they could carry, put each man's silver in the mouth of his sack, and place Joseph's silver cup in the mouth of Benjamin's sack. The steward did as Joseph said. As morning dawned, the men were sent away with their donkeys. They had gone only a short distance from the city when the steward caught up with them and accused them of returning evil for good. The cup from which his lord drank and by which he practiced divination was missing. The steward asked why they had done this evil thing.

The brothers answered that they had brought back the silver found in their sacks from Canaan. How then could they steal silver or gold from the steward's master's house? If any servant was found with the cup, he would die, and the rest would become slaves. The steward narrowed the sentence: the one found with the cup would be Joseph's slave, and the rest would be blameless.
Each brother lowered his sack quickly and opened it. The steward searched, beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest. The cup was found in Benjamin's sack.

The brothers tore their clothes. Each man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city. Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house while Joseph was still there, and they fell before him to the ground. Joseph asked what deed they had done and whether they did not know he could practice divination. Judah answered that God had found out the guilt of Joseph's servants. What could they say? How could they clear themselves? They were Joseph's slaves, both they and the one in whose hand the cup had been found.
Joseph said that would be far from him. Only the man with the cup would be his slave. The rest could go up in peace to their father.
Then Judah stepped close and put his own life in the gap.

He retold the story as Joseph already knew it and as their father lived it. Judah spoke of the old man in Canaan whose life was bound up with Benjamin's life. Joseph's brother was dead. Benjamin alone was left of his mother's children, and their father loved him. If the boy did not return, their father would die. His gray head would go down to Sheol in sorrow. Judah reminded Joseph that he had guaranteed the boy's safety to his father. If Benjamin did not go back with him, Judah would bear the blame to his father all his days.

"Now please let your servant stay here as my lord's slave in place of the boy. Let him return with his brothers. For how can I go back to my father without the boy? I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him."

Joseph could no longer control himself before all who stood by him. He cried for everyone to leave his presence. No Egyptian was with Joseph when he made himself known to his brothers. Joseph wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard and Pharaoh's household heard. Then Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?"
His brothers could not answer him, because they were dismayed at his presence.

Joseph told them to come near. He said he was Joseph, their brother, whom they had sold into Egypt. Then he gave them a way to survive the truth. "And now, do not be distressed or angry with yourselves that you sold me into this place, because it was to save lives that God sent me before you."

The famine had been in the land for two years, and five years remained in which there would be neither plowing nor harvest. Joseph said God had sent him before them to preserve a remnant on earth and to keep alive many survivors. "Therefore it was not you who sent me here, but God, who has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his household and ruler over all the land of Egypt."

They were to hurry back to Jacob and tell him to come down without delay. Jacob would dwell in the land of Goshen, near Joseph, with his children, grandchildren, flocks, herds, and all that he had. Joseph would provide for them there, because five years of famine were still to come. They were not to fall into poverty, Jacob or his household or all that belonged to him.
Joseph fell on his brother Benjamin's neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck. Joseph kissed all his brothers and wept over them. After that, his brothers talked with him.

The report reached Pharaoh's house that Joseph's brothers had come, and it pleased Pharaoh and his officials. Pharaoh told Joseph to load their animals and go to Canaan, bring their father and households, and come back. Pharaoh would give them the best of the land of Egypt, and they would eat the fat of the land. Wagons were to be taken for their wives and little ones. They were not to be concerned about their goods, for the best of all the land of Egypt was theirs.

Joseph gave them wagons according to Pharaoh's command and provisions for the journey. To each man he gave changes of clothes. To Benjamin he gave 300 pieces of silver and five changes of clothes. To his father he sent donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt, grain, bread, and provisions. Then Joseph sent his brothers away, and as they departed, he told them not to quarrel on the way.

The brothers went up from Egypt and came to Jacob in Canaan. They told him Joseph was still alive and that Joseph was ruler over all the land of Egypt. Jacob's heart stood still because he did not believe them. But when they told him all the words Joseph had spoken, and when Jacob saw the wagons Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of Jacob revived. Israel said it was enough. Joseph was alive. He would go and see him before he died.

title: Goshen, Blessings, and Burial
subtitle: Genesis 46 to 50, Berean Standard Bible
description: Jacob's family settles in Egypt, final blessings and burial, and Joseph's farewell.
paragraphs: Israel set out with everything he had, and at Beersheba the old promise met him before Egypt did.

Jacob offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. God spoke to Israel in visions of the night and called his name twice. Jacob answered that he was there. God said He was the God of Jacob's father. Then God told him, "Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you into a great nation there. I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back. And Joseph's own hands will close your eyes."

Jacob left Beersheba. His sons carried him, their wives, and their little ones in the wagons Pharaoh had sent. They took their livestock and the goods they had acquired in Canaan, and Jacob came into Egypt with all his offspring. Genesis names the sons, grandsons, daughters, and granddaughters who made the journey. The text counts seventy persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt.

Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to Jacob, fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a long time. Israel told Joseph he was ready to die, since he had seen Joseph's face and knew Joseph was still alive.

Joseph told his brothers and his father's household that he would go up and report to Pharaoh. They had come from Canaan, and they were shepherds who had kept livestock from their youth. When Pharaoh called them and asked their occupation, they were to say exactly that. Joseph had a reason for the plain answer. Every shepherd was detestable to the Egyptians, so Pharaoh would let Jacob's household settle in the land of Goshen.

Joseph chose five brothers and presented them to Pharaoh. Pharaoh asked their occupation. The brothers answered that they were shepherds, as their fathers had been. They had come to live in Egypt for a while because the famine was heavy in Canaan and there was no pasture for their flocks. They asked to live in Goshen. Pharaoh spoke to Joseph. The land of Egypt lay before him. Joseph was to settle his father and brothers in the best of the land, in Goshen. If Joseph knew capable men among them, Pharaoh wanted them put in charge of Pharaoh's livestock.

Joseph brought in Jacob and presented him before Pharaoh. Jacob blessed Pharaoh. Pharaoh asked Jacob how many years he had lived. Jacob replied, "My travels have lasted 130 years." Then he added, "My years have been few and hard, and they have not matched the years of the travels of my fathers." Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and went out from his presence.

Joseph settled his father and brothers and gave them a possession in the best of the land, in the district of Rameses, as Pharaoh had instructed. Joseph provided food for his father, his brothers, and all his father's household according to the number of their children.

Now the famine tightened on people who did not have Joseph's storehouses in the family. There was no bread in all the land, for the famine was very severe. The land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished because of the famine. Joseph gathered all the money found in Egypt and Canaan in exchange for the grain people bought, and he brought the money into Pharaoh's house.

When the money from Egypt and Canaan was gone, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and asked for bread. They did not want to die in his presence because their money had run out. Joseph told them to bring their livestock, and he gave them food in exchange for horses, flocks, herds, and donkeys. He supplied them with food that year in exchange for all their livestock.

When that year ended, the people came again. They would not hide from Joseph that their money was gone and their herds had been given to him. Nothing was left before him except their bodies and their land. They asked Joseph to buy them and their land for bread. They would be servants to Pharaoh, and Pharaoh would give them seed so they might live, not die, and so the land would not become desolate.

Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh. Every Egyptian sold his field because the famine was severe on them. Joseph reduced the people to servitude from one end of Egypt's border to the other. Only the land of the priests he did not buy, because the priests had a fixed allowance from Pharaoh and ate from that allowance. Joseph told the people he had bought them and their land for Pharaoh. He gave them seed for planting. At harvest, a fifth belonged to Pharaoh. Four fifths were theirs for seed, food, and their households. The people said Joseph had saved their lives. They asked to find favor in his eyes and said they would be Pharaoh's servants. Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt, still in place when Genesis was written: a fifth belongs to Pharaoh. Only the priests' land did not become Pharaoh's.

Israel settled in Egypt, in the land of Goshen. His household acquired property there. They were fruitful and multiplied greatly. Jacob lived in Egypt seventeen years, so the years of Jacob's life were 147.

When the time drew near for Israel to die, he called Joseph and made him swear an oath. Joseph was not to bury him in Egypt. When Jacob slept with his fathers, Joseph was to carry him out of Egypt and bury him in their burying place. Joseph said he would do as Jacob had spoken. Jacob told him to swear, and Joseph swore. Then Israel bowed himself on the head of the bed.

After this, Joseph was told that his father was ill. He took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and went to Jacob. Israel strengthened himself and sat up in bed. He told Joseph that God Almighty had appeared to him at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed him there. God had promised to make him fruitful, multiply him, make him into a company of peoples, and give the land to his offspring after him as an everlasting possession.

Jacob adopted Joseph's sons. Ephraim and Manasseh would be Jacob's, just as Reuben and Simeon were his. Children born to Joseph after them would be Joseph's and would be called by the names of their brothers in their inheritance. Jacob remembered Rachel, who had died in Canaan on the way when there was still distance to go to Ephrath. He had buried her there on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.

Israel's eyes were heavy because of old age, and he could not see. When he saw Joseph's sons, he asked who they were. Joseph said they were the sons God had given him in Egypt. Jacob told Joseph to bring them near so he could bless them. Joseph brought them near, and Jacob kissed them and embraced them. Israel told Joseph he had not expected to see Joseph's face, and God had let him see his offspring too.

Joseph took Ephraim with his right hand toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh with his left hand toward Israel's right hand, because Manasseh was the firstborn. He brought the boys near. "But Israel stretched out his right hand and put it on the head of Ephraim, the younger; and crossing his hands, he put his left on Manasseh's head, although Manasseh was the firstborn."

Israel blessed Joseph through the boys and spoke of the God before whom Abraham and Isaac had walked, the God who had been his shepherd all his life to that day, and the angel who had redeemed him from all evil. He asked that the boys be blessed, that his name and the names of Abraham and Isaac live on in them, and that they grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth.

When Joseph saw that his father had laid his right hand on Ephraim's head, it displeased him. He took hold of his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head. Joseph told him Manasseh was the firstborn and should receive the right hand. His father refused. Jacob said he knew. Manasseh would also become a people and would be great, but his younger brother would be greater than he. Ephraim's offspring would become a multitude of nations. Israel blessed them that day and set Ephraim before Manasseh.

Israel told Joseph he was about to die, but God would be with Joseph and his brothers and would bring them back to the land of their fathers. Jacob also gave Joseph one portion more than his brothers, a portion Jacob said he had taken from the hand of the Amorites with his sword and bow.
Then Jacob called his sons to gather around so he could tell them what would happen to them in days to come. The blessing at the bedside became twelve different futures.

Reuben, Jacob's firstborn and the beginning of his strength, heard that he would no longer have the preeminence. He had been turbulent as the waters, and he had gone up to his father's bed and defiled it. Simeon and Levi were paired as brothers whose swords were weapons of violence. Jacob cursed their anger, fierce and cruel, and said they would be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel. They would not share a single inheritance in one place.

Judah stood taller in his father's words. His brothers would praise him. His hand would be on the neck of his enemies, and his father's sons would bow down to him. Judah was a lion's cub and a lion who stooped down. No one would dare rouse him. Jacob said, "The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his." Judah's foal would be tied to the vine, and his garments washed in wine and the blood of grapes.

Zebulun would dwell at the shore of the sea and be a harbor for ships, with his border beside Sidon. Issachar was a strong donkey lying between sheep pens. He saw rest was good and the land pleasant, so he bent his shoulder to bear a burden and became a servant at forced labor. Dan would judge his people as one of Israel's tribes, a serpent by the road and a viper by the path that bites the horse's heels so its rider falls backward. In Dan's line Jacob paused and said, "I await Your salvation, O LORD."
Gad would be raided by a raiding party, but he would raid at their heels. Asher's food would be rich, and he would yield royal delicacies. Naphtali was a doe set free that gives beautiful words.

Joseph received the longest blessing after Judah. He was a fruitful bough by a spring, with branches running over the wall. Archers bitterly attacked him, shot at him, and harassed him. But his bow remained steady, and his arms were strengthened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, by the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel. Jacob spoke of the God of his father who helped him, the Almighty who blessed him with blessings of heaven above and the deep that crouches beneath, blessings of the breasts and of the womb. The blessings on Joseph surpassed the blessings of Jacob's parents, reaching to the boundaries of the everlasting hills. They rested on Joseph's head, on the prince among his brothers.
Benjamin was a ravenous wolf. In the morning he devoured the prey. At evening he divided the spoil.

All these were the twelve tribes of Israel, and this was what Jacob spoke to them when he blessed each with the blessing appropriate to him. Then Jacob charged them about his burial. He was about to be gathered to his people. They were to bury him with his fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite, the cave in the field at Machpelah near Mamre in the land of Canaan, the field Abraham had bought from Ephron as burial property. Abraham and Sarah were buried there. Isaac and Rebekah were buried there. Leah was buried there. When Jacob had finished commanding his sons, he drew his feet into the bed, breathed his last, and was gathered to his people.

Joseph fell on his father's face and wept over him and kissed him. Joseph commanded the physicians in his service to embalm his father. The physicians embalmed Israel, taking forty days, the time required for embalming. The Egyptians wept for Jacob for seventy days.

When the days of mourning had passed, Joseph spoke to Pharaoh's household. He asked them to tell Pharaoh that his father had made him swear to bury him in the tomb Jacob had prepared in Canaan. Joseph asked permission to go up, bury his father, and return. Pharaoh told him to go up and bury his father, as he had sworn.

Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of Pharaoh's household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt. Jacob's whole household went, and Joseph's brothers, and his father's household. Only their little ones, flocks, and herds were left in the land of Goshen. Chariots and horsemen also went up with him. It was a very great company.

When they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, they lamented there with a very great and grievous lamentation. Joseph made a mourning for his father seven days. The Canaanites who lived in the land saw the mourning at Atad and said it was a grievous mourning for the Egyptians. The place was called Abel-mizraim, the Mourning of Egypt. Jacob's sons did for him as he had commanded them. They carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field at Machpelah, near Mamre, the field Abraham had bought from Ephron the Hittite as burial property. After he had buried his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and all who had gone up with him.

Once Jacob was buried, Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead. They said Joseph might bear a grudge and pay them back in full for all the evil they had done to him. They sent a message to Joseph saying their father had commanded before he died that Joseph should forgive the transgression of his brothers and their sin, because they had done evil to him. They asked Joseph to forgive the transgression of the servants of the God of his father. Joseph wept when they spoke to him.

His brothers also came and fell down before him. They said they were his servants. Joseph told them not to fear. He asked whether he was in the place of God. Then Joseph gave Genesis its clearest sentence about the pit, the prison, and the throne.
"As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this, to preserve the lives of many people."
Joseph told them not to fear. He would provide for them and their little ones. He comforted them and spoke kindly to them.

Joseph remained in Egypt, he and his father's household. Joseph lived 110 years. He saw Ephraim's children to the third generation. The children of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were also raised on Joseph's knees. Joseph said to his brothers that he was about to die, but God would surely attend to them and bring them up out of that land to the land He had sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Joseph made the sons of Israel take an oath: "God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place."
So Joseph died at the age of 110 years. They embalmed him, and he was placed in a coffin in Egypt.
Genesis ends in Egypt, with Jacob buried in the promised land, Joseph's coffin still waiting, and God's promise pointed beyond the border.
